network.overall_strategy: Valine is treated as a skeleton-limited target. The network therefore uses two experimentally strong end-games: surface Strecker/hydrolysis from isobutyraldehyde and hydrothermal metal-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate. Upstream, three spark-discharge contexts generate an HCN plus branched-carbonyl pool, acetone can also enter the Patel-Sutherland cyanosulfidic sequence to valine aminonitrile, and a compressed pyruvate-to-alpha-ketoisovalerate branch is included explicitly as the major speculative bottleneck. Competing diversion of isobutyraldehyde to pantoic acid and of alpha-ketoisovalerate to alpha-hydroxyisovaleric acid are retained because both are emphasized limitations in the literature. Ten representative pathways to valine are listed.

reactions.name: Classic Miller-type spark generation of HCN and branched carbonyls

conditions.other: Reducing CH4/NH3/H2O vapor with lightning-like discharge and condensed aqueous trap

reactions.mechanism: Plasma-generated radicals from methane/ammonia/water form HCN and a mixed aldehyde/ketone pool that is trapped in condensate.
reactions.reasoning: Classic spark-discharge experiments are the clearest prebiotic demonstration that valine-relevant carbonyl precursors can arise from simple reduced gases. The cited studies directly detected valine in discharge residues and interpret amino-acid formation through gas-phase production of HCN plus aldehydes/ketones followed by aqueous cyanide chemistry; here the discrete acetone and isobutyraldehyde nodes represent that inferred precursor pool rather than directly tabulated yields. This route is strongest in local reducing settings and weakens in more oxidized atmospheres (Ring et al., 1972; Johnson et al., 2009; Schlesinger and Miller, 1983).

reactions.name: Volcanic aspirator spark generation of HCN and branched carbonyls

conditions.other: Steam-aspirated volcanic plume analog with gas recycling and aqueous trap

reactions.mechanism: Recycled discharge chemistry in a steam-rich plume broadens the HCN plus carbonyl precursor pool before products are quenched into water.
reactions.reasoning: Reanalysis of Miller's volcanic aspirator apparatus showed substantially greater amino-acid diversity and yield than the classic setup, consistent with plume recycling and steam injection enhancing the same HCN/carbonyl pool needed for valine. As in rxn_001, assigning specific acetone and isobutyraldehyde nodes is a mechanistic condensation rather than a directly tabulated experimental concentration (Johnson et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2009).

reactions.name: Sulfur-rich spark/plume generation of HCN and branched carbonyls

conditions.other: Sulfur-bearing volcanic plume analog; additional H2S-bearing gases are implicit rather than expanded as separate nodes

reactions.mechanism: Sulfur-bearing discharge chemistry generates the same general HCN plus carbonyl precursor ensemble under more volcanic conditions.
reactions.reasoning: H2S-rich or sulfur-bearing discharge experiments increase reduced organic diversity and C4 amino-acid production, making sulfur-rich plumes a plausible alternative source of the HCN plus branched-carbonyl pool feeding valine. The exact acetone/isobutyraldehyde output is not directly reported for this variant, so this node is partially inferential and more contested than rxn_001-002 (Parker et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2008).

reactions.name: Acetone cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Evaporitic or ferrocyanide-release setting to raise local cyanide activity

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds reversibly to the ketone carbonyl to give the cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Acetone cyanohydrin is a documented entry point into the cyanosulfidic valine-precursor network. The chemistry is straightforward, but ocean-scale HCN was likely too dilute, so this step is placed in concentrated surface settings rather than the open ocean (Patel et al., 2015; Stribling and Miller, 1987).

reactions.name: Cyanosulfidic homologation from acetone cyanohydrin to valine aminonitrile

conditions.other: 254 nm UV, sulfide-rich surface pools, staged delivery; sulfide reagents are implicit rather than expanded as separate nodes

reactions.mechanism: Overall lumped cyanosulfidic sequence: sulfide converts cyanohydrin-derived intermediates to thioamide-type species, Cu/UV photoredox drives deoxygenative reductive homologation to the isobutyraldehyde-level nitrile pool, and ammonia furnishes the aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is the most experimentally complete feedstock-to-valine-precursor route in the literature: Patel et al. showed access from acetone through cyanosulfidic chemistry to the valine aminonitrile, and later thiophosphate photochemistry preserved the same network logic. However, discrete valine-aminonitrile yields were not reported, and the need for high sulfide, 254 nm UV and staged reagent delivery remains a major plausibility critique (Patel et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2023; Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Aqueous Strecker synthesis of valine aminonitrile from isobutyraldehyde

conditions.other: Mildly basic to neutral pools; evaporation or freezing favored to concentrate cyanide

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine/iminium with the aldehyde, then cyanide adds to give the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: The Strecker end-game from isobutyraldehyde to valine aminonitrile is one of the most robust pieces of valine chemistry in the literature and is fully consistent with the classic spark interpretation of valine formation. The main uncertainty is not this step but the prior supply of isobutyraldehyde and sufficiently concentrated cyanide (Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013; Ring et al., 1972; Stribling and Miller, 1987).

reactions.name: Ferrocyanide-enabled aerosol Strecker synthesis of valine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Aqueous aerosol or droplet chemistry, UV-exposed, Fe(II)-rich setting

reactions.mechanism: The same Strecker sequence operates as in rxn_006, but cyanide is buffered and released from Fe-cyanide solids or aerosols rather than being supplied only as free dissolved HCN.
reactions.reasoning: Ruiz-Bermejo et al. demonstrated prebiotic Strecker syntheses of valine under aerosol conditions using ferrocyanide or Prussian Blue as practical cyanide storage and release media. This is important because primitive-ocean HCN is expected to have been too dilute for efficient Strecker chemistry without local concentration or storage (Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013; Stribling and Miller, 1987).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of valine aminonitrile to valine

conditions.other: Prolonged hydrolysis during wet-dry or geothermal cycling

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration and hydrolysis convert the aminonitrile to the alpha-amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolytic release of amino acids from cyanide-derived precursors is a standard final step in prebiotic amino-acid chemistry, including valine-forming Strecker systems. This step is slower than aminonitrile formation but chemically straightforward under repeated heating and hydration (Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013; Pulletikurti et al., 2022).

reactions.name: Speculative nonenzymatic pyruvate-to-alpha-ketoisovalerate sequence

conditions.other: Represents pyruvate homocoupling to acetolactate plus reductoisomerization and dehydration at mineral interfaces under geothermal cycling

reactions.mechanism: Lumped hypothetical sequence corresponding to pyruvate homocoupling, reductoisomerization and dehydration to alpha-ketoisovalerate.
reactions.reasoning: This reaction is explicitly speculative and represents the major bottleneck in valine prebiotic chemistry. The biological pyruvate -> acetolactate -> dihydroxyisovalerate -> alpha-ketoisovalerate sequence is known, but the provided literature reports no peer-reviewed nonenzymatic demonstration of the skeleton-building steps; it is included to expose the gap rather than to claim experimental support, and it is likely rate-limiting if such a branch exists at all (Keefe et al., 1995; Muchowska et al., 2019; Kaur et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Ni-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate

conditions.other: pH about 8; cool vent-mixing zone placement to limit thermal degradation

reactions.mechanism: Alpha-ketoisovalerate first forms an imine/iminium with ammonia, then metal-assisted hydrogenation yields valine; competing direct carbonyl reduction gives the alpha-hydroxy acid.
reactions.reasoning: Direct valine formation from alpha-ketoisovalerate, ammonia and H2 is experimentally strong, and no conversion occurs without a metal catalyst. Kaur et al. showed Ni catalysts give both valine and a substantial alpha-hydroxy acid byproduct, which is captured here as mol_015. The network places this step in cooler H2-rich vent-mixing settings rather than hotter fluids because amino acids and intermediates degrade at elevated hydrothermal temperatures (Kaur et al., 2024; Aubrey et al., 2009).

reactions.name: Fe-Ni meteoritic reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate
agents: ground Fe-Ni meteorite / native metal alloy

conditions.other: pH about 8; metal grains or meteoritic dust at water-rock interfaces

reactions.mechanism: Fe-Ni metal surfaces catalyze imine hydrogenation from alpha-ketoisovalerate and ammonia, while parallel reduction furnishes alpha-hydroxyisovalerate.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. demonstrated that ground Aletai iron meteorite catalyzes H2-driven reductive amination of biological alpha-ketoacids including alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine. This is one of the most geochemically defensible catalytic end-games because meteoritic Fe-Ni metal and native alloys are plausible natural catalysts, but the unresolved prebiotic problem remains the supply of alpha-ketoisovalerate itself; cooler settings are again favored to reduce decomposition (Kaur et al., 2024; Aubrey et al., 2009).

reactions.name: Pantoic acid diversion from isobutyraldehyde

conditions.other: Neutral to mildly basic pool chemistry with wet-dry concentration

reactions.mechanism: Formaldehyde addition and cyanohydrin chemistry divert the branched aldehyde toward pantoate chemistry; the node is drawn as pantoic acid, the hydrolytic equivalent of pantolactone-family products.
reactions.reasoning: Isobutyraldehyde is not valine-specific feedstock and is also a documented precursor to pantoate chemistry. Miller and Schlesinger reported pantoic acid from isobutyraldehyde plus formaldehyde and HCN, and Fairchild et al. later showed phosphate-catalyzed selective diversion of the glycine/valine Strecker aldehydes toward pantolactone-family products at neutral pH. This branch is included because it directly competes with valine synthesis for the same branched aldehyde pool (Miller and Schlesinger, 1993; Fairchild et al., 2024).

pathways.name: Classic spark to aqueous Strecker valine
pathways.description: Local reducing discharge chemistry generates HCN and isobutyraldehyde, which undergo catalyst-free aqueous Strecker chemistry and hydrolysis to valine.

pathways.name: Classic spark to ferrocyanide-buffered Strecker valine
pathways.description: The same classic discharge precursor pool is routed through aerosol/ferrocyanide-mediated cyanide storage before hydrolysis to valine.

pathways.name: Classic spark to cyanosulfidic valine aminonitrile
pathways.description: Spark-generated acetone and HCN feed the cyanosulfidic Patel-Sutherland branch to valine aminonitrile, which then hydrolyzes to valine.

pathways.name: Volcanic aspirator spark to aqueous Strecker valine
pathways.description: A plume-recycling spark source produces the same key HCN and isobutyraldehyde pool, followed by aqueous Strecker chemistry and hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Volcanic aspirator spark to ferrocyanide-buffered Strecker valine
pathways.description: Volcanic-plume discharge products enter the ferrocyanide-aerosol Strecker variant before hydrolysis to valine.

pathways.name: Volcanic aspirator spark to cyanosulfidic valine aminonitrile
pathways.description: The plume-enhanced discharge route supplies acetone and HCN for the surface cyanosulfidic sequence, ending in aminonitrile hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Sulfur-rich spark to aqueous Strecker valine
pathways.description: A sulfur-bearing plume/discharge source provides the same branched aldehyde pool, which is then converted to valine by the Strecker-hydrolysis end-game.

pathways.name: Sulfur-rich spark to cyanosulfidic valine aminonitrile
pathways.description: Sulfur-bearing discharge products feed directly into the sulfide/UV-driven cyanosulfidic branch and then hydrolyze to valine.

pathways.name: Speculative pyruvate branch plus Ni reductive amination
pathways.description: A metabolism-like but explicitly speculative pyruvate-to-alpha-ketoisovalerate branch is followed by experimentally demonstrated Ni-catalyzed reductive amination to valine.

pathways.name: Speculative pyruvate branch plus Fe-Ni meteoritic reductive amination
pathways.description: The same speculative alpha-ketoisovalerate supply branch is finished by experimentally demonstrated Fe-Ni meteoritic metal catalysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Conceptually aligned with the classic Miller-to-Strecker route and with literature reporting valine in spark-discharge products. The pathway is weakened because rxn_001 is an unbalanced product-pool shorthand rather than a chemically defined reaction, rxn_006 should release H2O as the Strecker byproduct, and rxn_008 should consume 2 H2O and release NH3/NH4+ to conserve mass. Transfer from spark products into aqueous surface chemistry is plausible but should be encoded explicitly.
suggestions: Replace rxn_001 with separate balanced spark/plume product-generation reactions or a product-pool node plus explicit transfer to water
Correct rxn_006 to include H2O as the Strecker byproduct
Rewrite rxn_008 as mol_008 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_012 + mol_002 (or NH4+ equivalent) and specify hydrolysis conditions

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The ferrocyanide-buffered Strecker concept matches literature attempts to address HCN dilution, but the encoding omits the ferrocyanide or Prussian Blue reservoir, aerosol context, and the water byproduct of Strecker chemistry. rxn_001 remains an unbalanced pool reaction, rxn_007 is missing H2O formation, and rxn_008 is not mass-conserving as written.
suggestions: Add an explicit ferrocyanide/Prussian Blue cyanide-storage node and aerosol or evaporation conditions
Correct rxn_007 to include H2O as the Strecker byproduct
Rewrite rxn_008 with 2 H2O consumed and NH3/NH4+ released

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is conceptually close to the Patel-Sutherland feedstock-to-valine-aminonitrile sequence, and rxn_004 is the only balanced step in the entire network. However, rxn_005 collapses a staged HS-/H2S, Cu photoredox, UV-driven sequence into one unbalanced surface reaction, so the key chemistry is not faithfully represented; rxn_001 and rxn_008 also need correction.
suggestions: Split rxn_005 into explicit cyanosulfidic substeps with HS-/H2S, Cu photoredox, UV, and staged reagent delivery
Keep rxn_004 as a separate cyanohydrin step but add the missing downstream intermediates instead of one lumped conversion
Rewrite rxn_008 with proper hydrolysis stoichiometry and conditions

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Among the listed routes this is the best aligned with literature arguments for localized reducing volcanic-plume or aspirator settings feeding aqueous Strecker chemistry. Even so, rxn_002 is still an unbalanced pool-forming surrogate, rxn_006 should release H2O, and rxn_008 is under-specified and not mass-conserving as written.
suggestions: Define the aspirator/plume chemistry with explicit gases, electrical energy, and balanced product-generation reactions
Correct rxn_006 to include H2O as product
Rewrite rxn_008 as aminonitrile hydrolysis with 2 H2O input and NH3/NH4+ output

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This route combines a plausible localized spark context with a literature-backed ferrocyanide-assisted Strecker end-game, but the actual reaction encoding is incomplete. rxn_002 is not a balanced chemical transformation, rxn_007 lacks the explicit ferrocyanide/aerosol chemistry and the H2O byproduct, and rxn_008 again fails stoichiometric conservation.
suggestions: Add explicit ferrocyanide-mediated cyanide release and aerosol conditions rather than only naming them in the reaction title
Correct rxn_007 to produce H2O
Specify the aminonitrile hydrolysis stoichiometry and conditions in rxn_008

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The route captures the literature idea that acetone can feed a cyanosulfidic branch to valine aminonitrile, but the key transformation is too compressed to be reliable as encoded. rxn_005 omits the sulfur reagent, copper photoredox catalyst, UV requirement, and staging; rxn_002 is an unbalanced spark pool shorthand; rxn_008 is not stoichiometrically complete.
suggestions: Decompose rxn_005 into literature-grounded substeps instead of a single unbalanced conversion
Specify the aspirator spark environment and balanced output chemistry in rxn_002
Correct rxn_008 hydrolysis stoichiometry and add hydrolysis conditions

suggestions: If this is a sulfur-rich spark/plume route, add explicit sulfur-containing feedstocks such as H2S and define the gas mixture
Correct rxn_006 to include H2O
Rewrite rxn_008 with proper hydrolysis stoichiometry and conditions

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This combines two sulfur-dependent ideas, but neither is encoded faithfully. rxn_003 is labeled sulfur-rich with no sulfur reagent present, and rxn_005 omits HS-/H2S, Cu, UV, and staged delivery; only rxn_004 is balanced. The path remains conceptually recognizable from the literature but chemically underdefined as written.
suggestions: Add explicit sulfur chemistry to rxn_003 or remove the sulfur-rich label
Replace rxn_005 with the actual multi-step cyanosulfidic sequence and reagents
Correct rxn_008 hydrolysis stoichiometry

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The alpha-KIV-to-valine end-game is literature-supported, but the route fails at the skeleton step. rxn_009 is both unbalanced and unsupported by published nonenzymatic evidence, and the environment label Biochemical is not a defensible prebiotic setting; rxn_010 also incorrectly makes valine and alpha-hydroxyisovaleric acid as stoichiometric co-products rather than alternative outcomes of reduction versus reductive amination.
suggestions: Either remove rxn_009 or decompose it into explicit pyruvate dimerization, reductoisomerization, and dehydration steps with literature support
Replace the Biochemical environment with a geochemically defined setting and justify transfer into the hydrothermal system
Split rxn_010 into separate competing reactions: alpha-KIV + NH3 + H2 -> valine + H2O and alpha-KIV + H2 -> alpha-hydroxyisovaleric acid, with Ni catalyst, pH 8, and H2 conditions

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Using Fe-Ni meteoritic material is geochemically imaginable and literature-backed for the final reductive amination step, but the pathway still depends on the same unsupported rxn_009. As written, rxn_011 also bundles valine formation and alpha-hydroxyisovaleric acid formation into one impossible stoichiometric event rather than treating them as competing product channels.
suggestions: Do not treat pyruvate -> alpha-KIV as a single reaction; provide explicit nonenzymatic steps or remove the branch
Specify the meteoritic catalyst context and transport logic into the hydrothermal setting
Split rxn_011 into separate competing valine and alpha-hydroxyisovaleric acid reactions with explicit Fe-Ni catalyst and H2 conditions

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is connected, has sufficient size, and is well aligned with the literature at the strategic level: it correctly treats valine as skeleton-limited, includes the two best-supported end-games (Strecker from isobutyraldehyde and metal-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate), and explicitly retains the pantoate and alpha-hydroxyisovalerate side sinks plus the unresolved alpha-KIV bottleneck. However, as an encoded reaction network it is not valid enough for approval. The deterministic balance check finds 11 of 12 reactions unbalanced; only rxn_004 is balanced. That alone severely lowers network validity and chemical feasibility. The main repair priorities are: rxn_001-rxn_003 should be replaced by balanced spark/plume product-generation reactions or by a separate product-pool abstraction with explicit transfer, and the checker suggests H2 is likely among the coproducts if these are retained as overall stoichiometries; rxn_003 is also labeled sulfur-rich despite having no sulfur-containing reactant. rxn_006-rxn_007 should release H2O as Strecker byproduct. rxn_008 should be written as mol_008 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_012 + mol_002 (or NH4+ equivalent). rxn_005 should not be patched with the checker's generic O2/CO2 hints; instead it needs to be decomposed into the actual Patel-Sutherland substeps with HS-/H2S, Cu photoredox, UV, and staged delivery. rxn_009 is both unbalanced and unsupported by current literature and should be decomposed into explicit referenced steps or removed. rxn_010-rxn_011 incorrectly combine valine and alpha-hydroxyisovaleric acid as co-products; they should be split into separate competing reactions with catalyst, pH, and H2 conditions. rxn_012 likely needs added water and NH3 release after cyanide capture/hydrolysis. Also fix the mol_008 structure or InChI inconsistency and add reaction-level citations tying individual nodes to the cited studies. No pathway is approvable in its current formalization, even though the conceptual literature framing is good.
